scene-u01-pnew1-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew1-5.text: Parameters without $m$: find the widest interval where $m$ stays constant, take its midpoint

scene-u01-pnew1-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew1-6.text: How to read: the left lists the three steps; the right shows source Example 16.6 sweeping the BMCA resolution parameter $r=1,\dots,77$; gray marks values whose $m$ the source does not report.

scene-u01-pnew1-12.name: text#12
scene-u01-pnew1-12.text: Record the number of clusters $m$ for each value

scene-u01-pnew1-15.name: text#15
scene-u01-pnew1-15.text: Find the widest interval with constant $m$

scene-u01-pnew1-16.name: text#16
scene-u01-pnew1-16.text: With real structure, $m$ stays stable for a long stretch

scene-u01-pnew1-19.name: text#19
scene-u01-pnew1-19.text: Take its midpoint as the parameter

scene-u01-pnew1-24.name: text#24
scene-u01-pnew1-24.text: Large enough parameters merge everything, so $m=1$ can stretch forever; set the range from the data scale first.

scene-u01-pnew1-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew1-26.text: Source Example 16.6: three groups of $100$ points, BMCA, $3\times3$ structuring element

scene-u01-pnew1-49.name: text#49
scene-u01-pnew1-49.text: (a) concludes three clusters; (b) the widest flat interval honestly says "it looks like one group"

scene-u01-pnew1-50.name: text#50
scene-u01-pnew1-50.text: Source: week15-v01 lecture lec15-kp04-relative-criteria §2 (Example 16.6 numbers from the source)

scene-u01-pnew1-51.name: text#51
scene-u01-pnew1-51.text: Only the two intervals given by the source

scene-u01-pnew2-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew2-5.text: Parameters with $m$: $J$ keeps falling, so look for the knee where it flattens

scene-u01-pnew2-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew2-6.text: How to read: both panels plot $J(m)/J(1)$ against $m$ ($N=200$); blue is $l=2$, orange is $l=8$; the left is four-group data, the right uniform data.

scene-u01-pnew2-90.name: text#90
scene-u01-pnew2-90.text: $k_m$ much larger than $1$: fast drop before $m$, almost none after, so a sharp knee

scene-u01-pnew2-91.name: text#91
scene-u01-pnew2-91.text: $k_m$ near $1$: a smooth curve with no knee

scene-u01-pnew2-92.name: text#92
scene-u01-pnew2-92.text: The source sets no numerical rule; $k_m$ is only for comparison

scene-u01-pnew2-95.name: text#95
scene-u01-pnew2-95.text: Misconception: "$J$ keeps falling, so pick the $m$ with the smallest $J$."

scene-u01-pnew2-96.name: text#96
scene-u01-pnew2-96.text: $J$ decreases monotonically with $m$ and is $0$ at $m=N$, so the minimum always means one point per group. Indices with a trend need a knee; only trendless ones (Dunn, DB) are read at their extremum.

scene-u01-pnew2-98.name: text#98
scene-u01-pnew2-98.text: Redo of Example 16.7 and $k_m$ computed by code [Added]

scene-u01-pnew3-5.name: text#5
scene-u01-pnew3-5.text: Higher dimension and more data sharpen the knee; in low dimensions structure is indistinguishable

scene-u01-pnew3-6.name: text#6
scene-u01-pnew3-6.text: How to read: each cell is $k_4$ for one setting (greener is sharper); rows are dimension $l$, columns data size $N$; the left table is four-group data, the right uniform data of the same size.

scene-u01-pnew3-95.name: text#95
scene-u01-pnew3-95.text: With structure: the knee at $m=4$ sharpens with dimension, and with more data even in low dimensions

scene-u01-pnew3-96.name: text#96
scene-u01-pnew3-96.text: Without structure: uniform data show no sharp knee

scene-u01-pnew3-97.name: text#97
scene-u01-pnew3-97.text: Redo: four groups $k_4$ from $2.2$ to $13.0$; uniform from $1.1$ to $4.0$

scene-u01-pnew3-100.name: text#100
scene-u01-pnew3-100.text: Failure: knees are judged by eye and overlap in low dimensions

scene-u01-pnew3-101.name: text#101
scene-u01-pnew3-101.text: In two dimensions with overlapping groups, four-group $k_4$ is only $2.2$ to $3.4$ while uniform data reach $4.0$, so the curve cannot tell them apart. Relative criteria only compare candidates; they cannot say whether a structure beats random.

scene-u01-pnew3-103.name: text#103
scene-u01-pnew3-103.text: Redo of Example 16.7 computed by code [Added]

steps.label: The widest flat interval
steps.speakerNotes: Without m: sweep the parameter and take the midpoint of the widest interval of constant m; Example 16.6 (a) has m=3 for r=37–67, so r=52; (b) has m=1 for r=7–46.

steps.label: The knee of J against m
steps.speakerNotes: With m: J decreases monotonically, so find the knee; four-group data with l=8 give k4=13.0, uniform data are smooth; never pick the m with the smallest J.

steps.label: When the knee is reliable
steps.speakerNotes: 16 settings: higher dimension and more data sharpen the knee; in two dimensions four groups give 2.2–3.4 and uniform up to 4.0, indistinguishable.
